strengths: Novel theoretical framework: First robust recovery algorithm for generic non-monotonic link functions (GELU, SWISH) beyond phase retrieval, closing a significant gap in the literature.

Strong technical contribution: Proves dimension-independent convex basin of constant radius around ground truth (Theorem 3.1) through careful Hessian perturbation analysis using Gaussian symmetry and higher-order moment bounds.

Elegant characterization: Introduces Expected Squared Convexity (ESC) condition as a higher-order analogue of monotonicity, naturally characterizing when second-order moments carry signal information.
Competitive complexity: Achieves near-linear time Õ(nd) and optimal sample complexity Õ(d) for robust recovery in non-convex setting, matching best known rates for non-linear models.
Broad applicability: Unified framework applies to 6 important link functions (logistic, tanh, probit, phase retrieval, GeLU, SWISH) with explicit numerical values demonstrating practical relevance.

Sophisticated technical approach: Elegant use of second-order Stein identities to decompose moment matrices, combined with robust spectral methods and hypercontractivity properties of Gaussian designs.
Comprehensive presentation: Well-organized paper with detailed proofs, complete algorithmic descriptions, code for computing constants, and transparent discussion of limitations.
weaknesses: Suboptimal error rate: Achieves O(σ√ε) vs information-theoretically optimal O(σε) for linear regression. No lower bounds provided to justify this gap or characterize hardness for general SIMs.

No empirical validation: Entirely theoretical work with no experiments validating whether constants are reasonable in practice, demonstrating algorithmic performance, or comparing with baselines—significant limitation for ICML.

Gaussian design restriction: All theory relies on X ∼ N(0, I_d); second-order Stein identities are inherently tied to Gaussianity. Sub-Gaussian or bounded covariate extensions appear fundamentally challenging.

Loose and complex constants: Spectral initialization requires m = Θ(C₄² · d log d/ε^{3/2}) with potentially large C₄; contamination threshold ε depends on multiple interacting factors (C₄, ESC, basin radius), making practical applicability unclear.
Very small convex basins for some functions: Phase retrieval has R ≈ 1.64 × 10^{-3} (extremely small). Small basin radii significantly impact initialization requirements and practical reachability.

Limited guidance on link function characterization: Incomplete discussion of which important link classes violate Assumptions 2.1-2.2, and connections to information exponent and computational-statistical gaps remain underexplored.

Complex algorithm with multiple stages: Two-stage approach (robust spectral initialization + gradient descent) adds implementation complexity; robust PCA subroutine is from concurrent work and practical deployment challenges (numerical stability, hyperparameter tuning) are unaddressed.

Spectral initialization error floor: O(ε^{1/4}) intermediate error suggests fundamental limitations in spectral methods alone, but analysis doesn't clarify whether this is tight or how it relates to problem hardness.
